title: Azerbaijan’s Lawyer Defends Defamation Suit Against CNN: ‘These Untrue Statements Actually Put Lives at Risk’
description: Azerbaijan is very upset about a June 5 report on CNN that Israeli troops had used the country as a staging area for attacks on Iran. The country’s
body:
Azerbaijan is very upset about a June 5 report on CNN that Israeli troops had used the country as a staging area for attacks on Iran. The country’s government says that the report, based on anonymous sources, is both completely wrong and dangerous, as it risks drawing Azerbaijan into the conflict.

	In this situation, most governments would issue a condemnatory statement and leave it at that. But Azerbaijan has gone a step farther, filing a defamation suit against CNN in Delaware last week. CNN’s response: “We stand by our reporting.”
	

	The complaint acknowledges that this situation is unusual, and admits that the First Amendment gives Americans the right to criticize their own government without fear of liability. But, it argues that the same logic does not apply to a foreign government, “which is not accountable to the American electorate.”


	To bring the case, Azerbaijan hired Wayne Dennison, a partner at Brown Rudnick who is best known for his work as part of Johnny Depp’s legal team in the case against Amber Heard.

	In an interview, Dennison defended the suit, saying that his client is entitled to recourse for reckless reporting. “These untrue statements actually put lives at risk,” he said.

	This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
	
		It would have been news to me that a foreign government would even think about suing for defamation, or that it would have standing to do that. How is that possible?	

	It’s long been clear that foreign sovereigns have the right to use the U.S. courts to redress harms that have been addressed to them. That’s a fundamental portion of the jurisdiction of our federal courts, and foreign governments have the opportunity to do this. With respect to this case in particular, what we’ve what we’ve looked at is we have a U.S. entity, CNN, engaged in activities that we think are improper and ultimately tortious. And the way in which this government will bring CNN to justice and ultimately to the table is to sue on CNN’s home court. Why’d you bring suit in the U. S.? Because that’s where the defendant is.
	
	
		From the journalism standpoint, obviously there’s a total right to criticize the United States government embedded in the Constitution, right? And I would think that U.S. citizens would also have pretty wide latitude in terms of criticizing foreign governments, too.	

	We’re not talking about criticism. What we’re talking about are direct, factual statements that relate absolutely to an ongoing war. CNN is making statements relative to my clients’ activities in a war that my clients absolutely unequivocally say are untrue. And the result of these untrue statements actually put lives at risk. I know you phrase this in terms of “criticism.” We’re not talking about criticism. What we’re talking about here are statements that — literally the way CNN attributes this is “somebody said,” right? They say “We have an unnamed source.” That is literally nothing more than “somebody said.” And frankly, if what they had reported was “Iranian officials say this,” or “Iran has taken the position that this occurred.” OK, then readers can assess for themselves whether these people are being truthful. But what we have is a report that is nothing other than “somebody said,” and I don’t think you ought to have the umbrella of the First Amendment to protect you from, “Hey, I heard this thing,” especially when you’re in a situation where people may die.
	
		In order to pursue this case, would you have to go get discovery from CNN — like, basically, “Tell me who your sources are.”	

	That may very well be where this ends up. And candidly, part of what you’re talking about here has always been one of the lesser holdings of New York Times v. Sullivan. And I think New York Times v. Sullivan has had some significant questions raised with respect to its continued viability, and this is a Supreme Court that seems far less interested in stare decisis than previous courts.
	
		You think there’s an openness to allowing some government claim of defamation, despite what New York Times v. Sullivan says about that.	

	It’s not the only claim. There’s a prima-facie tort allegation under Delaware law. But the ultimate issue is that we very much expect to be able to go forward and to allege that if your sole reliance as a news organization is on an argument that “somebody said” — and the reporter, with respect to this, has a known history of anti-Azerbaijani reporting — that maybe you got to do a little more, as a news organization.
	
	
		I hear your argument. I would wonder about a chilling effect. Think of foreign dissidents coming to the U.S. and speaking out against their home government. If Iran can come into U.S. courts and sue people who criticize its government, even if what they say is ridiculous and false, it feels like opening a door that you might not want to open.	

	Yeah, and again, I understand the use of the word “criticism.” They made a factual statement that we believe to be — and we believe we can prove to be — untrue. And it’s a factual statement that literally throws an entire country in the middle of a war. At some point, whatever the issue is, you got to look up and say, “Hey, I got to get this right.” I don’t know how to look at it any other way.
	
		If this gets to trial, you will have to show somehow that, in fact, Israeli troops were not staged in Azerbaijan.	

	I assume that they are going to raise as a defense, truth, because that’s a complete defense to defamation. We will then establish that what they reported was untrue, which in fact it was untrue.
	
		You spoke about the peril here. But in terms of the harm suffered, is there a way to quantify the harm to the government of Azerbaijan in terms of dollars from this report?	

	We haven’t made a damages estimate. And candidly, as we proceed, it’s unclear what the damages are going to be. The damages have been very, very significant in terms of international relations. But I can’t tell you to the dollar what the ultimate number is going to be. Frankly, one of the things that we have asked repeatedly from CNN, including in the complaint, is to simply retract the article. And thus far, that that’s been met with either silence or resistance.

schema.headline: Azerbaijan’s Lawyer Defends Defamation Suit Against CNN: ‘These Untrue Statements Actually Put Lives at Risk’

title: ‘Survivor’ vs. ‘The Traitors’: Will Emmy Voters Finally Give the Original Reality Juggernaut Its Due?
description:
“The Traitors” has won more Emmys in three years than “Survivor” has won in 25.

	It’s not close, either. Since arriving on Peacock, Alan Cumming’s
body:
“The Traitors” has won more Emmys in three years than “Survivor” has won in 25.

	It’s not close, either. Since arriving on Peacock, Alan Cumming’s Scottish castle whodunit has banked eight total Emmys — a casting win before it ever cracked the marquee race, back-to-back reality competition trophies in 2024 and 2025, two hosting wins for Cumming and a Creative Arts sweep in 2025 that added cinematography, directing and picture editing in a single cycle. CBS’ long-running “Survivor,” the show that made all of this possible, owns five. That includes Jeff Probst’s four consecutive hosting Emmys from 2008 to 2011 and a 2010 cinematography win. The trophy that matters most, however — outstanding reality-competition program — has eluded it since the Television Academy created the category.
	

	And let’s be clear about why the category exists at all.




	

									Robert Voets/CBS
	



	When “Survivor” premiered in the summer of 2000, it drew 51 million viewers to its season finale, which crowned Richard Hatch the first-ever Sole Survivor. The Academy created the reality competition program Emmy in 2003, in direct response to the boom “Survivor” ignited. Then it handed the inaugural trophy to its CBS sister series “The Amazing Race.” “Survivor” lost to “The Amazing Race” four straight times from 2003 to 2006, before it did something stranger than losing: It completely disappeared.

	For 16 consecutive years, the biggest brand in the genre couldn’t even get nominated — from 2007 through 2022. That stretch included the “Cook Islands” and first Fiji seasons (Seasons 13 and 14), which crowned Yul Kwon — in the first season to feature a final three instead of a final two, a format that coincidentally included Season 50 contestant Ozzy Lusth — and Earl Cole, who became the first unanimous winner in the show’s history.
	

	During that drought, “The Amazing Race,” “The Voice” and “RuPaul’s Drag Race” took turns building dynasties. When the new-era “Survivor” finally clawed back into the field in 2023, it lost to “RuPaul’s Drag Race.” It took another year off before returning in 2025, only to lose to “The Traitors.”

	An interesting note is the reality-competition Emmy has gone to a Mark Burnett production four times — all for “The Voice.” The category has spent two decades rewarding the man who helped define the genre while conspicuously never rewarding the show that made him.

	So here we are again, coming off a celebratory 50th season — “In the Hands of the Fans” — that crowned Aubry Bracco over runners-up Jonathan Young and Joe Hunter in an 8-3-0 jury vote and awarded a record-setting $2 million grand prize.

	“The Amazing Race,” a nominee in every eligible year of the category’s existence except the pandemic-scrambled 2020 ceremony, missed the cut entirely for only the second time ever. ABC’s “Dancing with the Stars,” riding its viral resurgence, is back in the race after an 11-year absence, chasing its own 0-for-10 correction.

	The case for “The Traitors” is that it has become the category’s auteur piece.

	Last year’s Creative Arts haul — directing, editing and cinematography — was the TV Academy telling us it doesn’t just enjoy the show; it admires the filmmaking. A third straight win would put it on the most exclusive shelf in reality television, joining “The Amazing Race,” “The Voice” and “RuPaul’s Drag Race” as the only shows to three-peat.

	Cumming, meanwhile, is chasing a hosting three-peat of his own, and the man he’d have to beat — for the third year running — is Probst. There’s a whole column in that proxy war alone: the tuxedoed theater lifer with two Tonys against the dimpled adventure guide who won this category’s hosting award the first four times it existed.

	The case for “Survivor” is the one the Emmys sometimes secretly love, and that’s the “overdue” correction.

	This is the Martin Scorsese- “The Departed” scenario — the institution that should have been honored in its prime, finally embraced late, with a milestone providing cover. “Survivor” hit Season 50 this spring, a fan-voted celebration of a quarter-century on CBS, exactly the kind of legacy moment that lets a voter feel like they’re honoring history rather than simply a season of television.
	

	Probst has spent the year as the genre’s beloved elder statesman. If there was ever a cycle for sentiment to beat momentum, it’s a 50th-season cycle.

	But sentiment has to overcome a structural problem: This category does not do lifetime achievement. It does dynasties.

	In 23 previous ceremonies, it has crowned exactly seven different shows. And once it falls for something, it falls hard — seven straight for “The Amazing Race,” four in five years for “The Voice,” four straight for “RuPaul’s Drag Race.” Television Academy voters — and this is a category voted on by the entire membership, rather than a specific peer group — aren’t correctors; they’re serial monogamists.



	

					THE TRAITORS — “The Death Conga” Episode 402 — Pictured: (l-r) Caroline Stanbury, Colton Underwood, Rob Rausch, Johnny Weir, Maura Higgins, Tiffany Mitchell, Candiace Dillard Basset — (Photo by: Euan Cherry/Peacock)
									Euan Cherry/Peacock
	



	Right now, they’re in love with a castle in the Scottish Highlands.

	Did enough of the all-stars fighting it out on the islands of Fiji build enough goodwill to get “Survivor” across the finish line?

	“Survivor” has outlasted every rival, every trend and every obituary written for network television. The one thing it has never figured out how to outlast is Emmy voters’ attraction to the newest game in town — a lesson it has now been taught by three different shows across three different decades.

	The torch, as Probst would say, represents life in the game. “Survivor” has kept its lit for 25 years — and will light a new one again this fall.

	On Sept. 14, we find out whether the Academy finally notices — or whether the castle drawbridge stays up for one more year. Voting closes Aug. 26 at 10 p.m. PT.

title: ‘How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days’ Sequel Set Up at Paramount; Kate Hudson to Produce (EXCLUSIVE)
description: A “How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days” sequel is in the works at Paramount, with original star Kate Hudson attached to produce the project, Variety can re
body:
A “How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days” sequel is in the works at Paramount, with original star Kate Hudson attached to produce the project, Variety can report exclusively.

	Development on the sequel is in early stages, with the cast and several key creative roles yet to be selected, according to a source close to the project. The intention of the filmmakers and the studio is to have Hudson and her co-star from the original, Matthew McConaughey, reprise their roles. The project is currently seeking a screenwriter, so casting will depend on the take.
	

	Stacey Sher is also on board to produce alongside Hudson through her Shiny Penny banner. Sher’s extensive list of producer credits includes “Pulp Fiction,” “Gattaca,” “Erin Brockovich,” “Vanilla Sky” and “Django Unchained.”


	Reps for Hudson and McConaughey did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment. 

	A follow-up to “How to Lose a Guy” seemed inevitable, considering the Y2K nostalgia wave washing over Hollywood right now. 2026 has so far brought “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” “Scary Movie” and “Toy Story 5,” all outsized box office hits that cashed in on late ’90s and early 2000s source material. The throwbacks aren’t slowing down either. “Practical Magic 2” and “Focker-In-Law” hit theaters soon, while “Shrek 5” and Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia” film are slated for 2027.

	Plot details for “How to Lose a Guy 2” are still being ironed out. The 2003 original followed the cat-and-mouse romance between magazine columnist Andie Anderson, played by Hudson, and McConaughey’s broish advertising executive Benjamin Barry. Andie, as research for an article about modern dating, seduces Benjamin and then transforms herself into the girlfriend from hell. Benjamin bets his boss he can make any woman fall for him, and Andie is his target. With a huge campaign on the line, he’s determined to make things stick. Of course, true love blossoms from the absurd circumstances. Donald Petrie directed the film. Supporting cast members include Kathryn Hahn, Adam Goldberg, Thomas Lennon, Michael Michele and Shalom Harlow. The film grossed nearly $180 million worldwide on a reported $50 million budget and is considered an essential title in the rom-com genre.
	

	Hudson’s most recent big-screen role was in 2025’s “Song Sung Blue,” for which she earned her second Oscar nomination. The first nod came for her iconic turn as Penny Lane in Cameron Crowe’s “Almost Famous.” She is also leading the sports comedy series “Running Point” for Netflix. While “How to Lose a Guy 2” has not been cast, Hudson’s role as producer makes it easy to believe she is in the wings, waiting for the right deal to bring her back.

	Of course, if Hudson were involved, McConaughey would presumably follow suit. The Oscar winner, who recently described “How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days“ as an “anchor” in the rom-com canon, has long been absent from the genre he was once closely associated with. He consciously distanced himself from romantic comedies in the 2010s, transforming his career with roles in critical dramas like “Mud,” “The Wolf of Wall Street,” “Interstellar” and “Dallas Buyers Club,” which earned him the 2014 Best Actor Oscar. He only recently ended a six-year big-screen hiatus with the release of “The Rivals of Amziah King.”

title: Wendy Williams Documentary Series ‘Clap If You Care,’ From the Host’s Longtime TV Producer, Picked Up at Peacock
description: Peacock is digging into the well-mined world of former radio host and TV talk show star Wendy Williams, greenlighting the three-part documentary “Cl
body:
Peacock is digging into the well-mined world of former radio host and TV talk show star Wendy Williams, greenlighting the three-part documentary “Clap If You Care: The Wendy Williams Show” (which is a working title) to air in 2027.

	Williams is not involved in the new docuseries, but her former producer is spearheading the project. As part of its announcement, Peacock confirmed that long-running “The Wendy Williams” show executive producer Susanne Bass, who ran that syndicated strip for 13 seasons, will also executive produce the documentary.
	

	“Her experience brings invaluable insight and a firsthand account of the show’s unique place in pop culture,” the press release said. “Clap If You Care: The Wendy Williams Show” is also executive produced by Ian Orefice, Jon Adler, Amanda Spain and Missy Walker for EverWonder Studio. Chris Witherspoon and Vanessa Golembewski are also EPs. 


	Williams was already a well-known radio star when she launched “The Wendy Williams Show” on TV in 2008. The series ended in June 2022, although the host had taken a leave of absence starting in 2021 due to medical issues related to lymphedema and Graves’ disease.

	The star entered a court-appointed guardianship in 2022, and in 2024, her team disclosed that she had been diagnosed with aphasia (affects language and communication abilities) and frontotemporal dementia, a disorder that impacts behavior and cognitive functions.

	Williams has been vocal about her objections to the guardianships, and her attempts to be removed from it. Just last week, a paparazzi took a video of Williams in New York, where according to the New York Post, she said, “I want out!” as she entered a building. Last year, she called into ABC’s “The View” and told her guardian Sabrina Morrissey and the judge who declared her “legally incapacitated” to “get off my neck,” declaring, “I need a new guardian.” Also last year, she told “The Breakfast Club” radio show that “I feel I’m in a prison” and “I am not cognitively impaired.”
	

	While past documentaries on Williams have focused on her health crises and guardianship, “Clap If You Care” appears to be more focused on the star’s career prior to the end of her show. The doc, according to Peacock, “celebrates the outrageous fun, cultural impact and meteoric rise of ‘The Wendy Williams Show.’”

	Here’s the full logline: “Skyrocketing from unlikely beginnings as a radio host to her impact on entertainment culture, Williams redefined the daytime talk genre with her outrageous on-screen fun on the long-running, Daytime Emmy-nominated talk show. While praising Williams’ TV reign, the documentary also sheds light on the complicated truths about the cost of fame and answers long-lingering questions surrounding the infamous exit from her own show. Over 20 former staffers from the talk show will share their behind-the-scenes experiences and memories of the pop culture icon.”

	Williams was an executive producer on Lifetime’s two-part docuseries “Where Is Wendy Williams?,” which chronicled her decline via footage shot between August 2022 and April 2023. It was a sequel of sorts to Lifetime’s 2021 documentary “Wendy Williams: What A Mess,” which looked at her public divorce and other public mishaps.

schema.headline: Wendy Williams Documentary Series ‘Clap If You Care,’ From the Host’s Longtime TV Producer, Picked Up at Peacock

title: Taylor Swift Recalls How ‘I Knew You Were Trouble’ Was Written As a ‘Really Sad Ballad’ in Grammy Museum Conversation Video
description: Taylor Swift opened up about the process of writing and recording her 2012 hit “I Knew You Were Trouble,” revealing that it was initially penned as
body:
Taylor Swift opened up about the process of writing and recording her 2012 hit “I Knew You Were Trouble,” revealing that it was initially penned as a “really sad ballad” before she was encouraged to incorporate dubstep.

	Swift reflected on the song’s creation during a Q&A at the Grammy Museum in Los Angeles last week, moderated by Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. The conversation, held as part of the Museum’s Icon Sessions, included Mason Jr. asking Swift how she prefers to build production around her lyrics and storytelling to create the “right mood and vibe.”
	

#TaylorSwift reveals that “I Knew You Were Trouble” started as a “sad piano ballad” until Max Martin and Shellback suggested, “What if it’s dubstep?”Swift adds that it ended up being “the best thing” that could have happened to the song.Watch the full Grammy Museum… pic.twitter.com/q3fhTLODw9— Variety (@Variety) August 24, 2026


	“It can either be compelling to make a song sound exactly how it feels or to flip it, which the people that really taught me the most about that are Max Martin and Shellback,” said Swift in a clip from the event. The best example of this, she noted, was “I Knew You Were Trouble,” which she originally had written as a “sad piano ballad.”


	“I was really excited to bring it in and I played them this really, really sad ballad and I was like I think just no drums and they’re like, ‘What if it’s dubstep?'” she recalled. “I was like I don’t know, guys. Let’s give it a run. I don’t know.”

	Swift explained that in the end, it “ended up being the best thing for it, and I think as a collaborator, my favorite people to be in the room with are ‘Yes, and?’ people. So why not try it. If they heard it and they thought dubstep, and I came to them specifically because I didn’t want to be making lateral moves creatively, why wouldn’t we go down that path? Why wouldn’t we? I really think that enthusiasm in the studio, it can really make or break what you end up creating.”
	

	“I Knew You Were Trouble” was part of a decided shift for Swift, who embraced a more pop-oriented sound on the song’s parent album “Red.” The experimentation paid off, as “Trouble” bowed at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 and inevitably reached a peak of No. 2.

title: ‘Insidious: Out of the Further’ Director Jacob Chase to Helm Horror Movie ‘Sleepover’ for Blumhouse Atomic Monster and Universal
description: “Insidious: Out of the Further” director Jacob Chase is set to direct the horror project “Sleepover” for Blumhouse Atomic Monster and Universal Pict
body:
“Insidious: Out of the Further” director Jacob Chase is set to direct the horror project “Sleepover” for Blumhouse Atomic Monster and Universal Pictures. Described as the “quintessential sleepover nightmare,” it’s set for an Oct. 8, 2027 theatrical release. 

	Chase directs from a screenplay co-written with “Night Swim” screenwriter Bryce McGuire, adapted from McGuire’s original short story. 


	Blumhouse Atomic Monster also presented Chase’s “Insidious: Out of the Further” along with Sony. The sixth installment in the “Insidious” franchise opened this past weekend to a solid $60 million worldwide. Chase has also directed “Come Play.” 
	

	Ahead of the “Insidious: Out of the Further” release, Chase told Variety, “Scaring people is kind of like magic — literally magic tricks — which is also something I had a real affinity for growing up,” he says. “It’s all misdirection, right? It’s figuring out how you can constantly surprise an audience in the way that the best magic tricks do.”


	Jason Blum will produce, while Chase, McGuire and Bea Sequiera serve as executive producers. Lilly Tyson will oversee the project for Blumhouse Atomic Monster.

	“Sleepover” is a Cinescape Entertainment production presented by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster. 

	Chase is represented by CAA, Gang, Tyre, Ramer, Brown & Passman, and The Initiative Group. McGuire is represented by Gersh and Ziffren Brittenham.

title: Warner Chappell Music Promotes Gabz Landman to Executive VP of A&R
description: Warner Chappell Music, the publishing arm of Warner Music Group, has announced the promotion of Gabz Landman to executive vice president of A&R. Bas
body:
Warner Chappell Music, the publishing arm of Warner Music Group, has announced the promotion of Gabz Landman to executive vice president of A&R. Based at the company’s Los Angeles headquarters, she will continue to report to Ryan Press, President of A&R for North America.

	Landman joined Warner Chappell in 2022 and has signed two-time Grammy songwriter of the year (and Variety Hitmakers 2024 songwriter of the year) Amy Allen, Laufey, John Ryan, Madison Beer, Lizzy McAlpine, the Chainsmokers, Delacey, Andrew Wyatt, Daniel Chetrit, Diplo and others.
	

	Landman works closely with Allen, who has scored hits with Olivia Rodrigo, Tate McRae, Sabrina Carpenter, and Olivia Dean. She set up the session for the global smash “So Easy (To Fall in Love),” pairing Allen, Dean, and John Ryan, and is currently working closely with Laufey, Diplo, and Madison Beer on upcoming music. Her inaugural signing, Cal Shapiro, has become a key collaborator with Cameron Whitcomb and Alex Warren, including on the hit single “Ordinary.” Another early signing, Carrie K, recently worked extensively on Noah Kahan’s album and celebrated her first No. 1 on Billboard’s Country Airplay chart alongside Koe Wetzel and Jessie Murph.


	Press said, “Gabz has a natural instinct for spotting and developing talent ahead of the curve, and she brings a 24/7 hustle to everything she does that’s rare to find. Having built some of the strongest relationships in this business, she’s a real advocate for artists and songwriters, and a true leader helping drive Warner Chappell’s growth, both on the charts and culturally. She’s earned this, and I couldn’t be prouder to see this next step.”
	

	Photo credit: Joelle Grace

schema.headline: Warner Chappell Music Promotes Gabz Landman to Executive VP of A&R

title: ‘Big Brother’ EPs and Host Julie Chen Moonves on Making 1,000 Episodes, Staying Competitive Against ‘The Traitors’ and the Chances of an All-Winners Season
description: This week, “Big Brother” will make history by being the first primetime show to hit 1,000 episodes. And in true “Big Brother” fashion, the show is c
body:
This week, “Big Brother” will make history by being the first primetime show to hit 1,000 episodes. And in true “Big Brother” fashion, the show is celebrating that milestone with a twisty, one-of-a-kind 90-minute episode that will air Thursday, Aug. 27.

	“It’s been really interesting and fun to think about how to celebrate the show,” executive producer Allison Grodner tells Variety. “We want to take some time at the beginning to really reflect on the past and, through fan engagement, have some fun reveals of polls that were taken of favorite moments, favorite winners and people that should have won.”
	

	Of course, the historic milestone comes as “Big Brother 28” is currently on the air. The popular reality program that airs three times a week on CBS is a one-of-a-kind social experiment where 16 strangers are locked in a house together for the summer. Each week, the houseguests compete for power and vote each other off. The catch is that not only are the houseguests completely cut off from the outside world, but everything they say and do is broadcast on the 24/7 live feeds.


	Julie Chen Moonves has been hosting the show since Season 1, which was a very different game back in 2000. Famously, the first season (which was run by the creators of the original Netherlands version) struggled with ratings. As rumors spread that the show would get canceled mid-season, so did criticism of Chen Moonves as a host.



	

					Julie Chen Moonves in 2002
									John Filo/CBS
	



	“I had such criticism from CBS News insiders, they were mad,” Chen Moonves says. “Andy Rooney was very upset that I was a CBS Morning News anchor and then, for 10 weeks, getting on a plane to Los Angeles to host an entertainment show. He went to the press saying that CBS News should immediately fire me. In his opinion, I was single-handedly blurring the lines between news and entertainment.”
	

	It wasn’t until Season 2 that the show took a page from the “Survivor” playbook by introducing more strategic elements, like the Head of Household competition, which determines who holds the power each week. The houseguests also started voting each other off that season.

	Those changes resulted in a more cutthroat “Big Brother,” causing a spike in the show’s popularity.

	“I tip my hat to them, because they were asked to take over a show in a genre that was very new then,” Chen Moonves says of executive producers Grodner and her Oscar-winning partner Arnold Shapiro, who worked on the show until Season 7. “They are the reason why it is still successful today, because they put in those basic rules to playing.”

	Rich Meehan joined as an executive producer in Season 5, and has been working closely with Grodner ever since.



	

					Rich Meehan and Allison Grodner in the “Big Brother 20” house.
									Sonja Flemming/CBS
	



	“It would be really hard if the people who haven’t lived this experience for all these years weren’t here to do the show; you’d start going down some of the same paths, which we already know are dead ends,” Grodner says.

	She continues: “Since we took off in Season 2, we’ve done well in the ratings, but it didn’t always guarantee that we were coming back the next year. Every single year in those first, maybe 10 to 15 seasons, at the end of the summer we’d go, ‘Are we coming back?’”

	Inside the CBS reality umbrella, it was about finding how to differentiate the show from “Survivor” and “The Amazing Race,” which all launched in the early 2000s as part of the craze that erupted from MTV’s “The Real World.”

	“We play in the comedy space, we play in the romance space. Obviously, the strategy and game are at the forefront, but there’s these other worlds we’re able to play in,” Meehan says. “If this is a show about people and it’s a microcosm of life, well, people are funny!”

	Since Season 2, the show’s overall format has stayed largely consistent over the years — the basic idea being that the houseguests have to outsmart their fellow contestants, vote them out and then convince everyone at the end why they should win $500,000 (upped to $750,000 starting in Season 23). The Power of Veto, introduced in Season 3, crucially gives nominees the chance to save themselves from the block before eviction night.
	

	But it wasn’t until Season 26 when the latest format change, the BB Blockbuster (then coined the A.I. Arena) added another dimension to the gameplay. Now, instead of two houseguests being nominated and only having one shot at safety, three houseguests are nominated every week; on live eviction night after the Veto is played, they go head-to-head to secure their safety.



	

					‘Big Brother 28’ houseguests compete in the BB Blockbuster.
									CBS
	



	“The current idea is that it’s like a new format piece for the live show, so I think, at least in the near future, it’s for sure something we’re going to continue to stick with, unless for some reason it stops working or generating,” Meehan says.

	The idea for the BB Blockbuster came from watching “Big Brother 20” contestant Kaitlyn Herman fail to complete a puzzle after she was given a chance to save herself as part of a big twist.

	“It captured so much energy and it was fun to watch. We were like, ‘How can we do that in the live show?’” Meehan says. “It’s super simple, but hey, increase the nominees and you’re making more enemies in the house, which creates more drama. And then also, we have this great ‘can’t miss’ sporting event that you have to watch. You don’t know who the final two up for eviction are until that moment.”

	After all, Big Brother’s motto is “expected the unexpected.”

	“We add in the twists and turns because more and more, you need those things that are promotable and you need those ‘can’t miss’ moments,” Grodner says. “We have what is the ultimate endurance competition in ‘Big Brother,’ just the whole season. Unlike other shows, we need to sustain interest for, in this case, 50 episodes.”

	Some fans prefer when the game has fewer twists that disrupt the natural flow of alliances and power structures. “But you also remember we’ve got so many seasons that the new cast can watch; we need to make sure that there’s still something to keep them on their toes, right?” Grodner says. “That there’s still going to be something unexpected.”

	On other reality shows, long-standing hosts have become more creatively involved behind the scenes over the years. Take Jeff Probst, the show’s host who also took over as showrunner 15 years ago.
	

	Chen Moonves says that’s not her lane.

	“I might suggest things, like ideas when we’ve had ‘Celebrity Big Brother,'” Chen Moonves says. “I like just being the host and not having that pressure of having to do creative or the casting.”

	Of all the reality TV fandoms, the “Big Brother” online community is one of the most active, largely incentivized through the show’s 24/7 live feeds. Like all fandoms, that comes with both enthusiasm and sometimes criticism of production.

	“We love the fans and their engagement, whether it’s passionate and opinionated, but we would be remiss if we produced a show based on just what’s happening on Twitter,” Grodner says. “And honestly, the creative for the show — how the summer is going to lay out and all that, for fairness reasons and so forth — is actually done well before the season starts. So those kinds of, ‘Oh, we’re adjusting something because of what’s being said online’ absolutely does not happen.”

	As a social experiment, “Big Brother” is also a microcosm of society. Because of the live feeds, everything the houseguests say gets recorded. Racist and homophobic comments over the years have made headlines — in the most extreme instance with Season 15, leading several houseguests to lose their jobs.

	The show has become more diverse since the 2020 CBS goal, which set a standard for the network’s unscripted shows to feature at least 50% people of color in the cast. Historically, Black people have struggled against the odds on “Big Brother.”

	“I remember when that mandate came down. I felt like, ‘Boy, at that point in history, we really needed it,'” Chen Moonves recalls.

	“It’s great, because anybody can win [now] — I don’t think there’s anything holding anybody back,” Meehan adds. Since Xavier Prather’s groundbreaking Season 23 victory, the show’s winners have all been people of color.

	Many show segments over the years have featured contestants talking openly about race, identity and how that shapes the way they navigate the game. Since the show casts complete strangers from different walks of life, watching them play against each other also leads them to learn from each other’s differences.

	“[Those conversations] happen more than ever, but there have been many in the history of the show. I remember Ken and Bunky [from Season 2]?” Meehan says. “What’s happening in the world is going to happen in the house. It’s just the nature of the show and that’s why people play the game differently now than they did 25 years ago.”
	

	As “Big Brother” nears another milestone with its upcoming 30th season, that also raises another question that many fans have been asking — will we ever see an all-winners season similar to what “Survivor” did with Season 40?

	Yet because “Big Brother” is a three-month commitment, that’s a lot tougher of a sell for even the most cherished vets. Chen Moonves has pitched multiple versions of an all-winners season over the years, although she’s made some tweaks.

	Her current take is multiple month-long versions of the game, akin to “Celebrity Big Brother.” One shortened season would bring back all the Season 1 houseguests to see how they’d play in the modern era of the show, while the next shortened season would group winners from different eras of the show.

	“I think if it’s shortened, everyone would be game. I haven’t heard of a past winner who’s bitter, who never wants to have anything to do with ‘Big Brother,'” Chen Moonves says.

	When looking to the future of “Big Brother,” some fans have speculated if Season 24 winner and “Big Brother: Unlocked” host Taylor Hale is being positioned to take on hosting duties were Chen Moonves to retire.

	“I’ve wondered that too because, to me, she would be perfect,” Chen Moonves says, praising her on-air skills from serving as an “Entertainment Tonight” correspondent.



	

					Jerry O’Connell, Taylor Hale and Derrick Levasseur hosting “Big Brother: Unlocked.”
									Matthew Taplinger/CBS
	



	Chen Moonves also pitches Season 16 winner Derrick Levasseur, as well as Jeff Schroeder and Jordan Lloyd from Season 11 and 13, as possible options.

	“But then I don’t know how the network would feel about, ‘Is it too close to home that they’ve walked in their shoes? Does that put them too much in a position of judgment?'” she says. “Part of me feels like maybe you want to keep the air pristine and have someone who comes from a news background. I got hired because I know how to do live interviews.”

	“But old-school journalists,” Moonves clarifies, referencing Anderson Cooper and Andy Cohen as potential options. “I feel a lot of journalists today go on the airwaves and I know exactly how they feel about an issue that they’re covering. To me, that’s not cool. Because then you have an agenda, you’re not really reporting.”

	The reality TV landscape has changed a lot since “Big Brother” premiered back in 2000. In recent years, “The Traitors” has dominated the online conversation around competition shows — and even cast “Big Brother” veterans like Danielle Reyes and Britney Haynes.
	

	“I do still think we are very unique, which is amazing to say that 28 seasons in, we still set ourselves apart,” Grodner says, adding that “Love Island” does have its own real-time element with how the episodes are structured. “But we dare to stream live and to have that other part of the show that people can interact with; no other show has done the live feeds to date.”

	Leaning into comedy and absurdity, Grodner says declaratively, is what makes “Big Brother” set itself apart tonally, and will ensure, she hopes, the show’s future far beyond Season 28 and the 1,000th episode.

	“Can any other show pull off a person in an egg suit, crying or screaming at someone at the nomination ceremony? And a teapot being banged around and have that become part of pop culture instantly?” Grodner says. “We can pull that off, but we can also pull off these amazing, compelling conversations. 

	“I think our range is unique, and I don’t know if any other show can encompass all of that,” she says. “I guess I dare them to!”

schema.headline: ‘Big Brother’ EPs and Host Julie Chen Moonves on Making 1,000 Episodes, Staying Competitive Against ‘The Traitors’ and the Chances of an All-Winners Season

body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	J.Crew is giving one of its most recognizable ’80s staples a Gen Z-sized makeover.

	The retailer has tapped Emma Chamberlain to front the launch of its new Tiny Rollneck, a shrunken, fitted take on the cotton sweater that has been a brand staple since 1988. The new silhouette officially drops Wednesday, Aug. 26 at 8 a.m. ET on jcrew.com.

	As its name suggests, the Tiny Rollneck tweaks the proportions of the original with a slightly cropped length and closer fit, offered in bright, graphic colors .The accompanying campaign, shot and directed by Ian Markell, places Chamberlain in a candy-colored, retro-futuristic world inspired by early-aughts fashion imagery and video-game character-selection screens. Chamberlain’s longtime stylist Jared Ellner worked with J.Crew creative director Olympia Gayot on the looks.



						
			
	

	
					

	The release is the latest chapter in J.Crew’s ongoing effort to put on its best-known archival pieces to a new generation. The original Rollneck debuted in the company’s 1988 catalog, distinguished by its heavyweight cotton knit, raglan sleeves and loosely curled neckline. Last fall, J.Crew put the sweater back in the spotlight with its “New Rollneck Generation” campaign, enlisting Benito Skinner, Molly Gordon, Maggie Rogers, Dominic Sessa, Lukita Maxwell, Rome Flynn and Taylour Paige-Angulo to model an assortment of new and archival-inspired versions. 

	J.Crew kept experimenting with the knit this spring with “Rollneck Remix,” its first designer-led reinterpretation of the staple. Timed to New York Fashion Week, the project handed the sweater over to five independent labels — Buci, Collina Strada, Eckhaus Latta, Patrick Taylor and Tanner Fletcher — which variously added lace, colorblocking, unconventional knit techniques and nautical detailing to its familiar shape.


	The J.Crew Tiny Rollneck collection launches Aug. 26 at 8 a.m. ET at jcrew.com.

schema.headline: Emma Chamberlain Brings a Gen Z Twist to J. Crew’s Signature Rollneck Sweater in New Campaign

title: Lindsay Clancy Judge Rejects Mistrial Bid in Murder Trial
description:
Lindsay Clancy
                          Judge Says No to Mistrial Bid
body:
Lindsay Clancy
                          Judge Says No to Mistrial Bid
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Lindsay Clancy will not be getting a mistrial ... after the judge shot down her defense team's request Monday following controversial testimony about religion.
      
    
            The drama unfolded during testimony from forensic psychologist Dr. Kirk Heilbrun, who brought up Clancy's belief that she and her children would be together in heaven ... and referenced Catholic teachings on suicide being a "mortal sin."
      
    
            Clancy's attorney immediately objected and asked for a mistrial, calling the testimony "over the top ... talking about religion, talking about heaven, talking about killing people and the impact it would have on Lindsay as well as her children."
      
    
            But Judge William Sullivan said no dice.
      

            He denied the mistrial request ... though he did reprimand prosecutors and told jurors Heilbrun's comments were "immaterial, irrelevant and to be disregarded."
      
    
            The jury was then sent home for the day.
      
    
            Clancy has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children -- 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan.
      
    
            Prosecutors say Clancy planned the killings ... while her defense argues she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time.
      
    
            If convicted, Clancy faces life in prison without parole.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman
                          Sister Fighting 'Unrestricted' Medical Exam ...
                          After Childhood Abuse Claims
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sam Altman and his sister are going back and forth in court over her submitting to a medical examination over her claims of childhood abuse ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs, Ann Altman is opposing the upcoming exam scheduled for August 26, claiming the conditions and scope of the exam were disclosed less than a week beforehand.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She said she never agreed to talk about anything other than her claims of suffering from PTSD, but says the doctor set to examine her is planning to assess "any mental disorder."
      

            Ann claims the physician plans to "cast a wide net and intrusively attempt to profile the entirety” of her mental health ... even including matters that she insists are unrelated to the issues in the case.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sam claimed the doctor had every right to grill Ann about her childhood abuse claims … saying she put her mental health and condition at issue in this suit by claiming she suffered psychological injuries due to his alleged abuse.
      
    
            The filing says the tech CEO believes Ann's allegations make an "unrestricted" clinical psychiatric interview warranted.
      
    
                    
                          
                                  
      
        
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Sam denied all claims he abused Ann when they were young. He claimed his family members defended him against the accusations.
      
    
            Sam countersued Ann for defamation but is only seeking $1 in damages.
